extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy (readers of Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting Aristotelian criteria for assessing moral character, self-control, pleasure, and friendship as laid out in Nicomachean Ethics (Books VII–VIII). Useful for evaluating virtue/vice distinctions and types of friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger vs Lust (moral disgrace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lust is more disgraceful than Anger because Lust does not follow Reason and yields to pleasure without Reason; Anger follows Reason in a manner and is more open and less insidious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts the two: Anger 'follows Reason in a manner' because it arises from a perceived insult and is open, whereas Lust 'does not' follow Reason and is therefore more disgraceful. Lust is insidious and pleasurable to the offender (no pain in insolence) while actions from Anger involve pain. Examples and poetic citations (Venus as 'weaver of deceits', Homer on the Cestus) are used to illustrate Lust's deceptiveness. Use these distinctions when judging which passions are morally worse: secrecy/insidiousness and yielding for pleasure mark greater disgrace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character who follows bodily pleasures in excess and in defiance of Right Reason, without acting on any deliberate conviction; contrasted with both the man of Self-Control and the man utterly destitute of Self-Control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: acts against Right Reason under passion; feels remorse (almost made up of remorse); may be curable (likened to acute disorders); admits two subforms (Precipitancy and Weakness). Examples: one who yields to laughter, Philoctetes wounded by a viper, people intoxicated by little wine. Assessment: degree of remorse, responsiveness to persuasion, and whether failure is due to habit or nature indicate culpability and curability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utter absence of Self-Control (confirmed vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who acts upon a conviction that it is proper to follow bodily pleasures without limit; such a person abides by his moral choice, lacks remorse, and is essentially incurable—a confirmed vicious character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from Imperfect Self-Control by the presence of a settled conviction that following the pleasure is right. Consequences: no remorse, permanence of the state (compared to chronic diseases), and greater overall danger because the highest principle is corrupted. Use permanence of choice and lack of remorse as diagnostic markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: A state in which the highest principle (reason) is preserved and one lacks desires contrary to Right Reason; such persons do not feel pleasure contrary to Reason and are distinct from both Self-Control and brute-like behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats this as the mean of moral excellence where desires are rightly ordered and the agent's dispositions align with reason. Not attributed to brutes (they lack deliberation). When evaluating character, look for absence of competing desires rather than mere resistance: Perfected Self-Mastery is not only not being conquered but not feeling the pull at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness vs Endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Softness: yielding to temptations or avoiding pain/effort when ordinary people can resist (includes Luxury); Endurance: continued resistance to pains or temptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Softness is characterized by seeking relaxation/rest (e.g., letting one's robe drag to avoid lifting it) and by being given to amusement; Endurance is sustained resistance. Self-Control (actual mastery) is preferred to Endurance (continued resistance) because mastery is a different and superior state. Use the agent's pattern (occasional yielding vs sustained resistance) to classify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precipitancy and Weakness (forms of Imperfect Self-Control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two forms of Imperfect Self-Control: Precipitancy—led by passion because resolutions were never formed; Weakness—made resolutions but do not abide by them due to passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperamental correlates: precipitancy common in sharp or melancholic temperaments (quick/violent passions), weakness where resolutions exist but fail. This distinction matters for remedial prospects: those who never form resolutions differ morally and therapeutically from those who break them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral blameworthiness criteria: motive, deliberation, and pain/pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of moral blame depends on whether an act is done from impulse, premeditation, or little/no impulse; acts done base without desire are judged worse than those done from strong desire, and actions done with pleasure (insolence) differ from those done with pain (anger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle holds that a man is worse for doing something base without impulse (or with slight impulse) than for doing the same out of strong desire, because the former suggests character defect rather than passion-driven failure. Also, actions committed with pleasure (insolence) are more disgraceful than those done under pain (anger). Use presence/absence/strength of desire, deliberation, and concomitant pleasure/pain to assess culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutishness (lack of moral choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state in which the subject lacks the moral principle entirely (no moral choice or deliberation); brutishness is less intrinsically bad than Vice but more to be feared because it lacks the highest principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle compares brutishness to inanimate vs animate beings: brute badness stems from absence of principle rather than corruption of it. Although such beings may be less harmful in some respects, they are more alarming because the moral principle is missing. Use absence of deliberative capacity and moral choice as diagnostic markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of pleasures (objects of moral states)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures differ: some are proper to the human race and natural in kind and degree, others brutish, and others caused by maimings/diseases; bodily pleasures and pleasures of the intellect differ in moral significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the first class (natural to humans) are objects of Perfected Self-Mastery; bodily pleasures (those accompanying desire and pain) tend to be the object of the man utterly destitute of Self-Control. Distinguish pleasures that are remedial (cures) from pleasures proper to a nature; the former do not make the agent morally choiceworthy in themselves. Use the nature/source of the pleasure (bodily vs intellectual; natural vs brutish/remedial) when evaluating moral targets of desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for when Pleasure is good
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure can be good 'per se' when it is an unimpeded 'active working' of a natural state (e.g., intellectual activity), not merely a process toward an end; some pleasures are choice-worthy though many bodily pleasures are low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle rebuts three views (pleasure not-good; most pleasures bad; pleasure not the chief good) by arguing that some pleasures are active workings akin to ends and that goodness may be relative/absolute. Assess pleasures by whether they are unimpeded active workings of a sound part of the soul (intellectual pleasures score highly) versus mere remedial or brutish pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons bodily pleasures seem most choice-worthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily pleasures appear most desirable because they drive out pain, often act as remedies, and are violent/strong impressions (e.g., youth, melancholic temperaments), but this appearance does not prove they're best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical and psychological factors (pleasure displaces pain, youth's constitutions, temperament) to explain popular error. When judging choices, correct for these biases: strong immediate relief does not equal highest moral value; evaluate the pleasure's relation to the full human good and its susceptibility to excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship: object-matter (good, pleasurable, useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship's objects are the good, the pleasurable, or the useful; friendship may be based on what is absolutely good or on what appears good to the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle raises whether friendship is grounded in objective good or in what is good for each person. For assessment: identify whether a particular friendship is motivated by mutual virtue (friendship for the good), mutual pleasure, or mutual utility; note that friendships based on virtue are highest and that legislators aim to secure friendship as the bond of communities.
